title-group.article-title: Stress, coping, and other determinants of poor sleep quality among healthcare students in a conflict region: a cross-sectional study

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Healthcare students face substantial academic demands that may impair sleep, increase stress, and shape coping behaviors. This study evaluated sleep quality, perceived stress, and coping strategies via the PSQI, PSS-10, and Brief-COPE and examined sleep quality predictors (demographic, stress-related, and coping factors) among healthcare students in a conflict-affected context.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This cross-sectional study surveyed Lebanese healthcare students (premedical, medical, nursing, pharmacy, and other health disciplines) via an online, self-administered questionnaire distributed through snowball sampling. Validated scales were used, and bivariate and multivariable analyses were conducted with the PSQI score as the dependent outcome.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 452 healthcare students, 77.2% reported poor sleep quality, 50% avoidant coping as their dominant strategy, and 92% reported moderate to high perceived stress. Being a nursing student (adjusted beta (95% CI) = 1.77 (0.19; 3.36)), a pharmacy student (1.08 (0.004; 2.17)), experiencing mental health problems (1.15 (0.42; 1.87)), social isolation (1.07 (0.17; 1.96)), having an avoidant-coping strategy (0.90 (0.19; 1.61)), or experiencing high perceived stress (1.14 (0.06; 2.76)) were positively and significantly associated with poorer sleep quality. However, exercising 3 times per week or more was positively associated with better sleep quality.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Poor sleep quality is widespread among healthcare students and is associated with increased stress, mental health issues, and avoidant coping. Supporting mental health, promoting adaptive coping, and encouraging regular physical activity may improve well-being in conflict settings to strengthen student health, academic performance, and the future healthcare workforce.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Healthcare students’ well-being is a growing concern, as demanding academic and clinical responsibilities can negatively affect sleep quality, increase stress, and challenge coping abilities. These interconnected dimensions are central to overall functioning and performance. While sleep quality refers to subjective satisfaction with sleep, such as duration and restfulness, stress is the body’s reaction to difficulties that might harm physical and mental health [1]. To manage stressors and maintain well-being, individuals rely on different coping strategies, such as relaxation techniques, problem-solving, and social support [2].

sec.title: Epidemiology of sleep disturbance
sec.p: Healthcare students around the world regularly report poor sleep and excessive stress levels. A 2023 systematic review of studies published between 2001 and 2023 across 31 countries revealed that 55.6% of medical students reported poor sleep quality, 33.3% reported excessive daytime sleepiness, and the average sleep duration was 6.5 hours [3]. Higher proportions have been reported in Arab countries such as Saudi Arabia, where 76% of medical students reported poor sleep and 53% perceived stress, with a significant positive association between both [1,4].

The situation is further exacerbated in conflict-affected regions, where healthcare students face, in addition to demanding academic duties, compounded stressors, including exposure to conflicts or wars, political instability, and disrupted academic schedules. In the Gaza Strip, 77.9% of students reported poor sleep quality and 65.2% reported high stress [5]. Similarly, a 2025 study in Lebanon found poor sleep quality in 73.5% of university students [6], with Lebanese medical students and residents, reporting high stress (87%) and disrupted sleep patterns (81%) [7]. These findings underscore the compounded impact of conflict on students’ well-being and highlight the need for targeted interventions to address sleep disturbances and stress in these settings.

sec.title: Determinants of poor sleep
sec.p: Multiple factors contribute to poor sleep quality among healthcare students and can be broadly classified into three categories: psychological, lifestyle/health-related, and sociodemographic. Psychological factors, including high academic stress, anxiety, and depression have been associated with impaired sleep [8,9]. Lifestyle factors such as nighttime screen use and caffeine consumption, as well as health-related factors such as chronic illnesses or preexisting mental health disorders, further disrupt sleep [8,10]. Moreover, sociodemographic characteristics, including female sex, low socioeconomic status, and employment in the healthcare field, have also been identified as significant predictors [11,12]. Collectively, these findings highlight the multifactorial nature of sleep quality in this population and underscore the importance of addressing psychological, behavioural, and health-related determinants.

sec.title: Coping strategies and their relationship to stress and sleep
sec.p: Accordingly, to manage stressors and enhance general well-being, individuals rely on different coping strategies. Coping is broadly defined as conscious thoughts and behaviours used to manage internal and external stressful situations [13]. Evidence suggests that coping style is meaningfully linked to sleep outcomes: A 2021 study revealed that active coping strategies, such as problem-solving or seeking emotional support, were associated with better sleep quality among nurses, whereas avoidant strategies, such as disengagement or denial, were linked to poorer sleep quality [2]. Moreover, stress can affect sleep quality both directly and indirectly, with the latter occurring through emotion-focused coping strategies [14]. Evidence from high-stakes medical training also links maladaptive coping and sleep disturbance to student performance. In a cross-sectional study of fourth-year medical students around an Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE), psychological well-being was negatively associated with avoidance coping and sleep disturbance, and OSCE performance was lower among those using avoidance strategies [15]. These relationships highlight the relevance of examining coping mechanisms alongside stress when studying sleep quality in healthcare students.

sec.title: Rationale in the Lebanese context
sec.p: In Lebanon, a country affected by compounded stressors, including the Beirut blast, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the economic collapse coupled with significant currency devaluation, stress and sleep quality have been examined as separate factors [6,16,17]; however, the associations with coping mechanisms among healthcare students remain underexplored. Assessing the predictors of sleep quality among healthcare students is of utmost importance, as inadequate sleep is strongly associated with mental distress, impaired learning, and increased clinical errors, ultimately compromising the students’ well-being. Conflict-related stressors further exacerbate these challenges, weakening workforce resilience. Identifying and addressing sleep problems can therefore help target prevention efforts, support mental health, and guide institutional and policy interventions to sustain healthcare services during and after crises.

sec.title: Study hypothesis and aim
sec.p: This study hypothesizes that healthcare students, including premedical, medical, nursing, or pharmacy students, experience significant sleep disturbances, elevated stress, and predominantly maladaptive coping strategies, which may compromise their physical and mental health, particularly in Lebanon’s challenging environment. The aim of this study was to assess 1) self-reported sleep quality via the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), 2) perceived stress via the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), 3) coping strategies via the Brief-COPE questionnaire, and 4) predictors of poor sleep, such as demographics, stress, mental health problems, and coping methods, in the context of ongoing crises in this conflict-affected region. This will ultimately inform interventions to prevent impaired learning.

sec.title: Study design, settings, and population
sec.p: A cross-sectional study was conducted between November 2024 and April 2025 after receiving approval from the institutional review board at the Lebanese American University (LAU.SOM.ZA1.22/Oct/2024). The target population consisted of university students enroled in healthcare-related programs at both private and public universities in Lebanon across different academic years and included students from the following disciplines: medicine, pre-medicine (biology, chemistry, and medical laboratory sciences), pharmacy, pre-pharmacy, nursing, medical laboratory sciences, speech therapy, physical therapy, nutrition, social work and dentistry.

sec.title: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sec.p: Students were eligible if they were currently enroled in a healthcare-related program at a Lebanese university during the study period, such as premedical, medical, prepharmacy, pharmacy, nursing, nutrition, laboratory sciences, physical therapy, speech therapy, medical social workers, dentistry, were aged ≥ 18 years, were able to complete the questionnaire in English or French. Students were excluded if they were not able to provide an electronic informed consent.

sec.title: Sample size calculation
sec.p: CDC’s Epi Info version 7.2.4 for population surveys was used to calculate the required sample size. A minimum sample size of 372 was required on the basis of an expected frequency of 58.7% poor sleep quality among Lebanese university students [18] to allow for 80% statistical power and to produce a 95% confidence level and an acceptable margin of error of 5%.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: An anonymous web-based questionnaire was developed in both English and French versions via Google Forms, as these are the primary languages of instruction in universities in Lebanon. The questionnaire was pilot tested among ten students. The final questionnaire was distributed to the healthcare students through a snowball technique and by relying on social media platforms. The study’s scope and purpose were clearly outlined at the beginning of the questionnaire. The participants were informed that their participation was voluntary, with assurances of anonymity and confidentiality. After they responded to the informed consent question, they completed the questionnaire.

sec.title: Measurement tools
sec.p: The questionnaire consisted of four sections. Section one concerned the participants’ demographic characteristics, including age, sex, field of study, physical activity, and chronic diseases, among others. Sections two to four assessed the participants’ perceived stress level via the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), their sleep quality via the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and their coping strategies via the Brief-COPE questionnaire.

sec.title: Description of the PSS
sec.p: The PSS-10 is a commonly used psychological instrument aimed at evaluating an individual’s perception of stress experienced over the preceding month. Upon further development, a 2012 review of the PSS’s psychometric evidence reported strong internal consistency and validity among both adult and university student populations [19], and the scale was subsequently validated among medical and health sciences students [20]. It has been used among Lebanese pregnant and postpartum women [21], university students [22], and, more specifically, nursing students [23]. The PSS-10 comprises 10 items, each of which is evaluated on a scale ranging from 0 (never) to 4 (very often). To compute the total score, the four positively phrased items (questions 4, 5, 7, and 8) were reverse-scored, and then the items were summed, resulting in a total score that ranged from 0 to 40, with higher scores signifying increased perceived stress. The scores are categorised as follows: low perceived stress (0 to 13), moderate perceived stress (14 to 26), and high perceived stress (27 to 40). The PSS focuses on perception rather than objective circumstances. Two individuals who have undergone similar life experiences may have different scores depending on their perceptions of and reactions to stress [24].

sec.title: Description of the PSQI
sec.p: The PSQI was established as a tool for measuring quality of life or disturbances in sleep during the past month. It is useful in clinical and research work for identifying sleep problems and assessing the efficacy of therapeutic interventions [25]. The PSQI has been validated among healthcare and medical students across diverse settings, showing acceptable internal consistency and stable test–retest reliability [26,27], and has been used among Lebanese pregnant women [21]. The PSQI comprises 19 self-rated items measured within seven subscales with scores varying from 0 (no difficulty) to 3 (severe difficulty). The components include subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, use of sleep medication and daytime dysfunction. The total score is obtained by summing the seven component scores and can range from 0 to 21. Higher scores are indicative of poorer sleep quality. Some studies categorised the scores as decent sleep quality (0 to 4) or poor sleep quality (≥5). This classification has been shown to distinguish between good sleepers and those exhibiting clinical levels of sleep disturbances [25].

sec.title: Description of the Brief-COPE
sec.p: The Brief-COPE is composed of 28 items designed to measure coping responses by which an individual handles stress [28]. It is a shortened version of the original COPE Inventory and is used in clinical and research settings to identify both adaptive and maladaptive forms of coping. The Brief-COPE has been validated among healthcare and medical students in various cultural contexts, showing acceptable internal consistency and good construct validity [29,30], and has been used among Lebanese university students [31].

Each item is rated on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (I haven’t been doing this at all) to 4 (I’ve been doing this a lot). The questionnaire measures 14 distinct coping strategies with two items per subscale. These strategies are categorised into three domains: problem-focused coping, emotion-focused coping, and avoidant coping. Although some validations (including the French version) describe alternative higher-order groupings, the Brief-COPE is fundamentally a 14-subscale instrument; therefore, we used a commonly applied analytic regrouping into three domains (problem-focused, emotion-focused, and avoidant) to enhance interpretability and maintain consistency with prior research [32]. Scores are calculated by averaging the scores of all items within a coping strategy or category. These total scores for each coping style indicate the frequency of use, with higher scores indicating greater use of a given coping strategy. Generally, problem-focused coping is associated with better psychological outcomes. Emotion-focused coping may alternatively be adaptive or maladaptive, depending on the situation. Avoidant coping is what usually results in worse psychological outcomes [28].

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The PSS, PSQI, and Brief-COPE scales and subscales were computed, and Cronbach’s alpha coefficients were calculated to evaluate internal consistency. Separate analyses of Cronbach’s alpha for the English (n = 421) and French (n = 17) versions showed that the English version had consistent reliability, while the small French sample produced unstable and low alpha values for PSQI and PSS (0.40–0.41), but higher values for the Brief COPE subscales (0.75–0.84). This reflects a statistical artefact: in very small samples, alpha is sensitive to scale length and item variability, making shorter, highly correlated subscales appear more stable than longer or more variable scales. Subsequently, the overall Cronbach’s alphas were reported, while acknowledging the presence of both language groups. Descriptive statistics were used to represent the students’ characteristics and scores and are presented as the means ± SDs or medians ± interquartile ranges when appropriate for continuous variables and percentages for qualitative variables. For descriptive purposes, the Brief-COPE coping domains (problem-focused, emotion-focused, and avoidant coping) were standardised to Z scores to account for differences in score ranges. For each participant, the domain with the highest Z score was considered his/her dominant coping style, which was then used to calculate the proportion of participants primarily using each coping style.

For the bivariate analysis of continuous variables, the normality of quantitative variables was assessed and verified via the Shapiro‒Wilk test, complemented by visual inspection of histograms and Q‒Q plots. Student’s t test was used to compare means between two groups, whereas ANOVA was applied for comparisons involving three or more groups after verifying homogeneity of variances via Levene’s test. When the assumption of homogeneity was violated, the corrected Student’s t test and the Welch test were used instead. For subgroups with a sample size smaller than 30 or when continuous variables were not normally distributed, nonparametric tests such as the Mann‒Whitney U test or the Kruskal‒Wallis test were applied. Additionally, Spearman correlation coefficients were used to examine the relationships between two continuous variables that were nonlinearly linked or not normally distributed.

A multiple linear regression was conducted to assess the associations between the dependent variable (PSQI) and potential confounders after verifying the assumptions of residual normality, linearity, homoscedasticity, and absence of multicollinearity to identify factors associated with the PSQI. The participants whose characteristics had a P-value less than 0.2 in the bivariate analysis (such as study field, physical activity, and coping scores) were included in the model. Regression coefficients ‘adjusted (β)’ and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported to quantify the associations between the PSQI score and the remaining variables.
An alpha of 0.05 was used to determine statistical significance. All analyses were performed via IBM’s Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 30.

sec.title: Participant characteristics
sec.p: A total of 452 participants were recruited. The majority were females (71%), with a median age of 22 years. Most of the participants were enrolled in private universities (86%). Approximately half of the participants reported that they either did not participate in physical activity or engaged in it only occasionally. In addition, 84% were non-smokers, 17% had a history of chronic diseases, and 23% reported mental health problems such as anxiety or depression as diagnosed by a physician. Furthermore, financial difficulties were reported by 32% of the participants, whereas 19% indicated experiencing academic challenges (Table 1).

sec.title: PSQI, PSS and Brief-COPE scales
sec.p: The Cronbach’s alpha coefficients for the PSQI and PSS were 0.67 and 0.72, respectively. For the Brief-COPE subscales, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficients were 0.87 for the problem-focused subscale, 0.86 for the emotion-focused subscale, and 0.79 for the avoidance-focused subscale. This reflects an acceptable internal consistency for the PSQI and good internal consistency for both the PSS and the Brief-COPE. The mean PSQI score (±SD) was 7.2 (±3.4), with 77.2% having a score greater than or equal to 5, indicating overall poor sleep quality. With respect to the Brief-COPE score, nearly half of the participants reported avoidant coping as their dominant strategy. Moreover, the PSS indicated that 92% of the participants reported a moderate to high perceived stress level, with 16% experiencing severe levels (Table 2).

sec.title: Bivariate analysis for the PSQI
sec.p: Statistically significant associations were found between the study field score and the PSQI score, with nursing students reporting the highest degree of sleep disturbance (mean PSQI score ± SD = 8.68 ± 3.58). Furthermore, living alone on weekdays or weekends and holidays, being a smoker, experiencing chronic diseases or mental health problems as diagnosed by a physician, financial difficulties, academic challenges, social isolation, break-up or family discord were associated with poorer sleep quality. Moreover, there was a significant but weak positive correlation between emotion-focused coping styles, avoidant coping styles, and poor sleep quality. In addition, participants with high perceived stress levels, as measured by the PSS, had the highest mean PSQI score. On the other hand, participants living with family on weekends and holidays and exercising regularly had significantly lower PSQI scores, reflecting better sleep quality (Table 3).

sec.title: Multivariable analysis for the PSQI
sec.p: The multivariable analysis revealed that being a nurse (adjusted beta (95% CI) = 1.77 (0.19; 3.36)) or a pharmacy student (1.08 (0.004; 2.17)), experiencing mental health problems as diagnosed by a physician (1.15 (0.42; 1.87)), social isolation (1.07 (0.17; 1.96)), having an avoidant-coping strategy (0.90 (0.19; 1.61)), or experiencing high perceived stress (1.14 (0.06; 2.76)) were positively and significantly associated with poorer sleep quality. Nonetheless, exercising 3 times per week or more was positively associated with better sleep quality (Table 4).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This first study in Lebanon examining sleep quality predictors alongside coping strategies revealed that healthcare students in a conflict-affected setting experienced significant sleep disturbances that were significantly associated with avoidant coping behaviour and high perceived stress levels. This observed association underscores the importance of targeted support strategies to strengthen student well-being and learning in conflict-affected settings.

sec.title: Sleep quality among healthcare students
sec.p: In the present study, poor sleep quality was reported by 77.2% of the healthcare students, with a mean PSQI score of 7.2, reflecting substantial sleep disruption. This is higher than the mean global PSQI score of approximately 6.1 and the pooled prevalence of 52.7% reported in a meta-analysis of medical students from Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and Oceania, indicating more pronounced sleep impairments in our sample [33]. This study findings exceed the high rates of poor sleep quality among healthcare students in the MENA region, where a 2025 systematic review reported a pooled prevalence of 59.1% [34]. In Saudi Arabia, the prevalence of insomnia among college students ranges from 19.3% to 98.7%, with a pooled estimate of 43.3% [35]. This finding was more pronounced when sleep disturbances were evaluated among medical students separately, with 98.7% experiencing insomnia symptoms and 70.5% experiencing poor sleep quality [36]. Additionally, the findings of the present study align with those of previous reports indicating that 73.5% of healthcare students in Lebanon experienced poor sleep quality during the war [6]. This underscores the need for targeted interventions to improve sleep quality and support student well-being in this conflict-affected context.

sec.title: Stress among healthcare students
sec.p: In this study, 92% of the participants reported moderate to high perceived stress, with 16% experiencing severe stress. The proportion of healthcare students experiencing high perceived stress varies by region but is notably elevated worldwide. A lower prevalence of stress was reported in European countries, where approximately 57% of healthcare students in Italy reported moderate stress levels and 6% reported high stress levels [37]. In Arab countries, 72.6% of Saudi Arabian students perceived themselves as stressed [38], with high levels affecting 13.7% of healthcare students [39]. Furthermore, 93% of Egyptian medical students reported moderate to high stress levels [40], which is in line with our findings. Stress is known to activate the hypothalamic‒pituitary‒adrenal axis, leading to high cortisol levels and sympathetic nervous system activity. Thus, poorly managed stress is associated with increased vulnerability to anxiety and depression [41]. Conflict settings further exacerbate stress. In Sudan, war-related psychological distress was common among medical students: approximately 28% experienced moderate distress, 29% experienced high distress, and nearly 30% experienced very high distress, reflecting the considerable mental health burden in this context [42]. This highlights the compounded burden of academic, social, and environmental stressors in conflict zones compared with more stable regions. Therefore, implementing structured stress-management or support programmes, such as mindfulness training or peer support groups, could help students manage stress responses, thereby promoting their well-being.

sec.title: Coping among healthcare students
sec.p: The most notable finding of the current study is that nearly half of the participants reported avoidant coping as their dominant style. Studies using the Brief-COPE among healthcare students have highlighted variations in coping strategies across cultural and contextual settings. In the United States and Europe, students mainly adopt problem-focused and active coping strategies such as planning and seeking instrumental or emotional support [43,44]. Furthermore, nursing students in the MENA region predominantly use problem-focused coping strategies, such as active problem-solving and seeking social support, as well as emotion-focused strategies, including positive reinforcement and turning to religion; on the other hand, they also rely on dysfunctional coping strategies, such as mental and behavioural disengagement [23]. Although a 2024 study among Lebanese adults revealed problem-focused coping to be the most commonly adopted strategy [17], the predominance of avoidant coping observed in the present study among healthcare students therefore represents a concerning pattern, underscoring the need to prioritise interventions that promote adaptive coping strategies to support students’ mental well-being.

Moreover, in situations characterised by high stress, particularly when stressors are perceived as uncontrollable such as conflicts, the effectiveness of coping strategies may depend on the association between perceived controllability and coping mechanism. Experimental evidence supports this ‘coping fit’ perspective, showing that approach-oriented coping is associated with greater positive affect under controllable health stressors [45]. However, previous research showed that greater reliance on avoidant coping is linked to poorer psychological and performance outcomes. Among medical students prior to an OSCE, avoidance was negatively associated with well-being, sleep, and exam performance [15]. In addition, in a 10-year longitudinal study, avoidance prospectively predicted higher stress exposure and depressive symptoms [46], and perceived stress has been shown to affect sleep quality indirectly via avoidance coping in adults [47]. These findings suggest that the high prevalence of avoidant coping in our sample may reflect a context-driven response to uncontrollable stressors, while sustained reliance on avoidance is generally associated with poorer well-being and sleep outcomes over time.

sec.title: Predictors of poor sleep quality
sec.p: In the present study, avoidant coping was significantly associated with worse sleep quality. These findings support earlier research among healthcare students showing that avoidant coping is associated with poorer stress management and disrupted sleep. In Europe and the United States, students who use problem-focused strategies, such as active problem solving, report better sleep quality, whereas reliance on avoidant strategies, such as behavioural disengagement or substance use, is associated with higher rates of sleeplessness and daytime fatigue [2,43,44]. In Arab countries, studies have shown that avoidant and emotion-focused coping, including denial and self-distraction, are significantly associated with higher PSQI scores and greater sleep disturbances [8,48]. In the Lebanese context, cultural and societal norms may affect healthcare students’ preference for avoidant coping mechanisms when experiencing high perceived stress. This is often shaped by stigma surrounding mental health, limited access to services, and societal expectations of self-reliance. In Lebanon, such stigma discourages individuals from seeking help, leading many to adopt coping strategies such as substance use or avoidance behaviours. Additionally, the normalisation of stress in demanding academic environments may further encourage the use of maladaptive coping strategies. These findings underscore the importance of considering cultural and societal contexts when addressing stress and coping mechanisms among healthcare students. Interventions should aim to reduce stigma, increase access to mental health services, and promote adaptive coping strategies tailored to the cultural norms of Lebanese society.

Students with high perceived stress had, on average, a 1.14-point higher PSQI score than did students with lower stress. Healthcare students worldwide face significant challenges related to stress and sleep quality, with variations influenced by regional contexts. In Europe, studies indicate that medical and nursing students often experience high levels of stress and poor sleep quality due to rigorous academic demands and long clinical hours. A study conducted among Italian medical students revealed that up to 62% of medical students reported poor sleep quality, which was associated with anxiety, depression, and stress and was often exacerbated by academic pressure [49]. Another study from Spain and Morocco reported that 54% of Spanish students and 81.7% of Moroccan students reported poor sleep quality, with nursing students generally experiencing less favourable sleep quality than medical students do [8]. The situation is likely exacerbated in Lebanon, where a 2025 study reported that 73.5% of university students had poor sleep quality, with those directly exposed to war exhibiting the highest levels of sleep disturbances [6]. These findings underscore the critical need for targeted interventions to address stress and sleep disturbances among healthcare students, particularly in regions facing unique challenges.

In the present study, nursing and pharmacy students had significantly increased PSQI scores, indicating worse sleep quality. This aligns with the literature indicating that nursing curricula and practices impose heavy sleep challenges. A Polish study, for example, revealed that the majority of nursing students have poor sleep quality, most likely as a result of stress and clinical shift work [2]. Similarly, pharmacy students frequently have to conduct many studies and tests. According to a US survey, approximately half of pharmacy students slept for less than seven hours on normal school nights and as few as five hours before tests, which is indicative of ongoing academic strain [50]. As a result, the sleep patterns of nursing and pharmacy students may be affected by irregular clinical hours and practical rotations, eventually disrupting their sleep patterns. Additionally, a greater proportion of female students and factors such as part-time work may further contribute to these differences compared with medical students, who often have more structured schedules, especially in preclinical years.

In the present study, a history of physician-diagnosed mental health problems, such as depression or anxiety, was significantly associated with worse sleep quality. This finding is consistent with previous literature linking mood disorders to insomnia. For example, Saudi healthcare students with higher levels of anxiety or depression are significantly more likely to experience sleep disturbances, with anxiety nearly doubling the likelihood of experiencing poor sleep [51]. In fact, mood disorders can contribute to heightened physiological and cognitive arousal, often leading to increased rumination and difficulty initiating sleep [52]. This finding emphasises the reciprocal relationship between poor sleep and psychiatric symptoms and highlights the need for early identification, targeted interventions, and support strategies to improve both mental health and sleep quality among healthcare students.

Feeling socially isolated was significantly associated with poor sleep. Social isolation and loneliness have been shown to reduce sleep quality. In fact, it has been reported that young adults who reported loneliness had lower subjective sleep quality and more daytime dysfunction than their non-lonely counterparts did, even after adjusting for depression and other variables [53]. The theorized explanation is that loneliness causes hypervigilance and stress due to increased cortisol, which may disrupt sleep [54]. This underscores the importance of social support for maintaining proper sleep patterns, as emotional encouragement and opportunities to share stress can buffer its effects, reduce rumination, and promote relaxation conducive to restorative sleep.

Moreover, engaging in regular exercise was significantly associated with improved sleep among healthcare students. This result is supported by a substantial body of evidence, including findings among Lebanese nurses, reporting that physical activity enhances sleep quality [55]. Exercising regularly may improve sleep quality by increasing sleep pressure, regulating circadian rhythms, and reducing stress [56]. Interventions aimed at increasing regular exercise could serve as an effective strategy to enhance sleep quality in healthcare student populations.

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: This is the first study to evaluate sleep quality, perceived stress, and coping strategies simultaneously among healthcare students in the context of Lebanon’s compounded and continuing crises, especially the economic crisis. Moreover, it documents the most dominant coping profile as being the avoidant one, reflecting how the future of the healthcare workforce is dealing with challenging or threatening situations, and support the development of tailored interventions to support healthcare students.

However, several limitations should be acknowledged. Participation was based on voluntary convenience sampling, which may have led to underrepresentation of certain subgroups, especially those that experienced poorer sleep quality or higher stress levels. Because recruitment relied on snowball sampling and open dissemination through student networks, an exact response rate could not be calculated. This approach may have introduced self-selection bias, potentially overrepresenting students more engaged with online platforms or more motivated to respond. Moreover, some specialties may be overrepresented, such as pharmacy students; however, this was accounted for in the multivariable analysis. Self-administered questionnaires may additionally be prone to reporting bias; however, the use of validated scales, such as the PSS-10, PSQI, and Brief-COPE, helps strengthen data reliability. Finally, despite statistical adjustments, unmeasured factors, such as prior mental health conditions, could still confound the observed associations.

sec.title: Practical implications
sec.p:
The observed associations have several practical implications for healthcare education, and student well-being. Enhancing sleep quality among healthcare students would require a multifaceted approach that addresses stress, social connectivity, and adaptive coping strategies. The following specific interventions are recommended:
Scheduling and work load management: The poor sleep quality among healthcare students, especially pharmacy and nursing students, suggests the need for targeted scheduling adjustments and workload management to reduce sleep disruption.
Mental health and stress support: The associations between poor sleep and mental health problems, social isolation, and high stress highlight the importance of integrating mental health support, peer networks, and stress management programs into curricula.
Coping strategies training: The association with avoidant coping underscores the need to train students in adaptive coping strategies tailored to the cultural norms of Lebanese society, such as reducing stigma, increasing access to mental health services and encouraging problem-focused approaches, to mitigate the negative impact on sleep.
Promotion of physical activity: The positive role of regular physical activity indicates that promoting exercise through structured programmes or campus initiatives may serve as a protective factor, improving sleep quality and overall well-being among healthcare students.
Student-focused interventions: Structured programmes such as PROMESS-Sleep (targeting sleep disturbances and fatigue) and PROMESS-Stress (focusing on psychological and physiological stress indicators) have been developed and may serve as models for intervention [57,58].
Participatory program development: Future initiatives could use a participatory qualitative approach, beginning with focus groups of students and faculty to identify needs and barriers, followed by co-construction workshops and pilot testing to design locally adapted interventions [59].

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Poor sleep quality is common among healthcare students, particularly in pharmacy and nursing programs, and is closely linked to high stress, mental health challenges, social isolation, and reliance on avoidant coping strategies. Encouraging adaptive coping strategies, mental health support, and regular physical activity could help mitigate these risks, enhancing both sleep quality and overall well-being. These findings highlight the need for targeted, context-sensitive interventions to support the mental health, resilience, and academic performance of future healthcare professionals, especially in high-stress or resource-limited settings. Future studies involving a random sample and, ideally, a longitudinal design could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the temporal relationships among stress, coping strategies, and sleep quality among healthcare students, especially in conflict zones.
